name: Alan of Lille
credit: Alanus doctor, woodcut portrait from an early printed book (Wellcome Collection, V0000079) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alan of Lille (Alanus ab Insulis) was a French theologian, philosopher and Latin poet of the twelfth century, born at Lille around 1128. He taught in Paris and perhaps at Montpellier, was known to his contemporaries as the “universal doctor”, and is said to have ended his life as a Cistercian at Cîteaux, where he died in 1202 or 1203.

His best-known literary works are the prosimetrum De planctu Naturae, in which Nature laments the vices of mankind, and the Anticlaudianus, a Latin hexameter epic in nine books in which Nature and the Virtues fashion a perfect man and Prudence ascends to heaven to obtain his soul. Composed in the early 1180s and answering the invective of Claudian’s In Rufinum, it was among the most widely read allegorical poems of the later Middle Ages.
